endorsements.quote: Governance should define who is responsible for AI selection, validation, monitoring, and clinical oversight, with mechanisms for investigating incidents and implementing corrective actions (33).

As AI tools assume partial or fully autonomous tasks, liability should be distributed proportionally among vendors, institutions, and clinicians based on their respective control over system behavior.
Policy should mandate standardized model cards, analogous to nutrition labels, for all medical AI systems (60).
Institutions must build capabilities for rigorous local validation precisely because transparency limitations prevent full assessment of vendor-conducted validation.

At minimum, these cards should specify the system’s intended clinical applications and users; training data sources and demographic distributions; validation metrics disaggregated by relevant subgroups with confidence intervals; and operational requirements.

Policy should establish tiered validation requirements mapped to intended use: standalone testing for triage applications, reader studies for detection and image generation/reconstruction devices, and prospective validation for autonomous systems (21).
Adaptive algorithms that learn through clinical use may require continuous validation with real-time performance monitoring and automated alerts when performance deviates from expected ranges.

Dual reporting pathways should be clearly defined: Vendors should report mandated events to regulators through MDR, while institutions should report directly to regulators when vendor responses are inadequate, ensuring critical information reaches oversight bodies even if one pathway fails.

Policy must require vendors to communicate clearly when updates occur, specify the channels through which updates will be announced, describe what has changed and why, and explain how performance differs from previous versions.
Postmarket oversight requirements should explicitly specify which clinician types are qualified to use imaging-related AI tools.
Radiologists bear responsibility for maintaining AI literacy and human–AI collaboration skills, including knowing when to trust versus verify recommendations (86,87).
Validation costs—personnel, infrastructure, and training—should be incorporated into funding mechanisms rather than treated as optional academic activities (70,71).

Providing systematic feedback about errors, near-misses, concerning patterns, or unexpected behaviors, including specific case details and comparative observations across populations, contributes valuable real-world evidence that complements formal performance metrics.

unlisted_practices: Require standardized dataset reporting cards with required fields for training demographics, pathology distributions, and acquisition parameters.
Mandate standardized validation reporting with disaggregated performance data in FDA 510(k) summaries.
Establish AI accreditation standards at the user or institution level setting minimum requirements for institutions deploying AI.
Require mandatory AI-specific postmarket performance reporting with defined metrics, disclosure triggers, and reporting frequency.
Fund public data repositories, centralized data pooling, and federated learning infrastructure tied to FAIR data sharing commitments.
Document agentic AI decision pathways and autonomy boundaries, including which tasks may be executed independently and where human authorization is needed.
Recognize AI oversight and validation activities as reimbursable professional services.
Support postmarket performance registries for aggregating AI performance data across institutions.
Clarify institutional rights regarding data ownership, intellectual property, and benefit-sharing when clinical data enable commercial AI.

screen.reason: This is a special report / policy commentary proposing a lifecycle-based governance and safety framework (translational bialignment) for AI deployment in radiology.
